Chemometrics & Applied Statistics

What is chemometrics?

Chemometrics applies statistical methods to chemical data to extract meaningful information and to support the design and interpretation of chemical experiments.
IUPAC Gold Book · chemometrics · DOI 10.1351/goldbook.CT06948

What is this course about?

AN ANALYTICAL QUESTION Three water samples are measured four times for nitrate. Which sample is clearly more contaminated, and how confident are we in that conclusion?
  • Sample C is much higher than A and B in this illustrative dataset.
  • Replicates reveal spread: a defensible conclusion needs both concentration level and variation.

Variables

Variable

In statistics, a variable is a characteristic or quantity that can take different values within a stated dataset, study, model or experiment. Its values may be observed, measured, assigned or controlled.
Introductory Statistics

Why do we need variables?

  • Describe experiments through individual aspects of a system.
  • Examine aspects separately, while stating the conditions.
  • Describe relationships between these aspects.

Variables, values, and observations

We prepare five calibration standards with chosen concentrations and measure their absorbance. Concentration and absorbance are variables. Each row is one observation of a calibration standard and each cell contains one variable value. The plot shows the same concentration–absorbance observations graphically.

Sampling locations and replicates

We sample one lake at five locations and take three replicate samples at each site. All 15 samples contain approximately the same concentration of analyte A. Each measurement is one observed concentration value, while the sampling site provides the grouping context.

Why do values differ?

DESIGNED VARIATION
We deliberately choose different values. |> Calibration standards: concentrations are assigned; absorbance is measured.
OBSERVED VARIATION
We measure differences rather than assign them. A variable's role depends on the study design. |> Lake samples: concentration may vary with the environment, sampling and measurement.

Observed variation has multiple sources

Describing the observed response

A_i = f(c_i) + \varepsilon_i
Aᵢ
Observed absorbance of measurement i
f(cᵢ)
Modelled response for the chosen concentration cᵢ
εᵢ
Combined effects not explained by the chosen model

From the example to a general model

y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i
yᵢ
Observed response of observation i
f(xᵢ)
Modelled response for the explanatory input xᵢ
εᵢ
Difference between the observed and modelled response; may combine several unmodelled influences

What can f(xᵢ) be?

Scalars, vectors and matrices

Illustrative concentrations in mg/L: samples A, B and C; nitrate and phosphate.
SCALAR
One number: nitrate in sample A.
\begin{aligned}x &= 2.55\\ x &\in \mathbb{R}\end{aligned}
VECTOR
One quantity across three samples: nitrate in A, B and C.
\begin{aligned}\vec{x} &= \begin{pmatrix}2.55\\3.14\\4.20\end{pmatrix}\\ \vec{x} &\in \mathbb{R}^{3}\end{aligned}
MATRIX
Rows: samples A, B, C. Columns: nitrate, phosphate.
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{X} &= \begin{pmatrix}2.55 & 0.80\\3.14 & 1.10\\4.20 & 1.60\end{pmatrix}\\ \mathbf{X} &\in \mathbb{R}^{3\times2}\end{aligned}

Types of variable values

The value type describes the entries, not the shape of their collection.
NUMBERS
Real: concentration in mg/L Integer: replicate count Complex: impedance in ohms
\begin{aligned}2.55 &\in \mathbb{R}\\3 &\in \mathbb{Z}\\2+3i &\in \mathbb{C}\end{aligned}
CATEGORIES
Sample classes: tap, lake, runoff Labels identify groups, not amounts.
c=\text{lake}
BOOLEAN
Quality check: passed or failed A condition is true or false.
\begin{aligned}b&=\mathrm{true}\\b&\in\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\end{aligned}

Mean Values

Why do we need mean values?

  • Summarize several values of a variable.
  • Represent many observations with one compact number.
  • Average comparable observations to reduce uncontrolled random fluctuations.

Example: Five dice make one experiment

Example: Five dice, one sum

Roll five fair dice and add their outcomes.

  • What average sum would you expect after many repetitions?
  • Can that average be a value that one experiment cannot produce?
set.seed(42)
dice <- sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)
list(dice = dice, sum = sum(dice))
set.seed(seed)
Sets the pseudorandom seed so this example can be reproduced.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws size values from x; replace = TRUE allows repeated die faces.
sum(x)
Adds the five sampled face values to obtain one experiment sum.
list(...)
Returns the named dice and sum values together.

Example: Different experiments, different sums

Illustrative sums from five repetitions (seed 42).
  • 10
  • 13
  • 18
  • 10
  • 23
  • Which value is the right one?

expected value

For a discrete random variable with finite expected absolute value, weight each possible value by its model probability, not by observed sample frequency.
\operatorname{E}[X] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}} x\,P(X=x)
X, E[X]
Discrete random variable and its distribution expectation.
x, S
x is one possible numerical value of X; S is the set of all possible values.
P(X=x)
Probability that X takes the value x. These model probabilities sum to 1 and weight the possible values; they are not observed sample frequencies.

Example: What do we expect from five dice?

ONE FAIR DIE
Six possible outcomes: 1 to 6 Each has probability 1/6.
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{E}[D]&=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}\\&=3.5\end{aligned}
D, E[D]
One fair die outcome and its expected value.
1…6, 1/6
Six faces, each with probability one sixth.
FIVE FAIR DICE
Add the five outcomes. Expectations add, too.
\begin{aligned}S&=D_1+\cdots+D_5\\\operatorname{E}[S]&=5\times3.5=17.5\end{aligned}
Dⱼ, S
Outcome of die j; S is the sum of five outcomes.
E[S], 3.5
Expected sum; each fair die has expectation 3.5.

Example: From a known model to measured data

THEORETICAL EXPECTATION
Fair-dice model: E[S] = 17.5. A probability-weighted, long-run average, not a required single outcome.
REAL OBSERVATIONS
Five experiment sums: 10, 13, 18, 10, 23. Finite random outcomes; each observed sum is an integer.
  • Why are the results different?
  • We can estimate the expected value from appropriately sampled real data.

arithmetic mean

\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
x̄, xᵢ
Arithmetic sample mean and observation i, in the same unit.
n, i, Σ
Sample size, observation index and sum over equally weighted numerical observations with meaningful addition. Normality is not required.

Example: Average five observed sums

Average five observed experiment sums, not all possible outcomes. The sample result need not equal the model expectation 17.5.
\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}{n}\\&=\frac{10+13+18+10+23}{5}\\&=\frac{74}{5}=14.8\end{aligned}
x̄, xᵢ
Average and observed sum from experiment i, not individual die faces.
n, i, Σ
Five equally weighted experiments; i indexes them; Σ adds their sums.

Example: Average five repeated experiments

Repeat the five-dice experiment five times.

  • List the sums and calculate their arithmetic mean.
  • Explain why a finite sample average need not equal 17.5.
set.seed(42)
sums <- replicate(5, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)))
list(sums = sums, mean = mean(sums))
set.seed(seed)
Makes the pseudorandom draws reproducible.
replicate(n, expr)
Evaluates expr n times and collects each experiment sum.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws five die faces from 1:6 with replacement.
sum(x)
Adds the five faces within one experiment.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of the five experiment sums.
list(...)
Returns the named sums and their mean together.

Example: Repeat the experiment more often

Compare averages from 5, 50 and 50,000 independent five-dice experiments.

  • Change the seed and repeat.
  • Does every larger sample have to be closer to 17.5?
set.seed(42)
sums <- replicate(50000, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)))
n <- c(5, 50, 50000)
data.frame(n, mean = sapply(n, function(k) mean(sums[seq_len(k)])))
set.seed(seed)
Fixes the pseudorandom sequence for reproducible comparisons.
replicate(n, expr)
Repeats the five-dice experiment 50,000 times.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws five fair-die outcomes for each experiment.
sum(x)
Adds the five outcomes in each repeated experiment.
data.frame(...)
Combines the repetition counts and their calculated averages as columns.
sapply(x, function)
Applies the supplied calculation to each repetition count.
function(k)
Defines a small calculation that receives one repetition count k.
seq_len(k)
Selects the first k experiment sums without exceeding the available data.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of the selected experiment sums.
c(...)
Combines the three repetition counts into one vector.

Example: Arithmetic means in water analysis

  • Oxygen: 8.6 mg/L
  • Nitrate: 3.4 mg/L
  • Iron: 5.0 mg/L

Calculate the mean of the Fe concentrations 5.2, 4.8, 5.1, 5.0 and 4.9 mg/L.

  • State the unit and the equal-weighting assumption.
fe <- c(5.2, 4.8, 5.1, 5.0, 4.9)
mean(fe)
c(...)
Combines the five measured concentrations into a vector.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of the five concentrations.

Example: Growth combines by multiplication

Example: Does arithmetic preserve growth?

ARITHMETIC FACTOR
Which constant factor reproduces 1600 cells from 100 in two equal periods? Apply it twice: 100 × m × m = 100m². Factor 5 predicts 2500 ≠ observed 1600. The arithmetic mean fails this growth question.
\begin{aligned}A&=(2+8)/2=5\\100\times5^2&=2500\ne100\times2\times8=1600\end{aligned}
A
Arithmetic average of growth factors 2 and 8: A = 5.
100, 2
Initial count 100; exponent 2 applies one factor over two equal periods.

geometric mean

G = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)^{1/n}, \qquad x_i > 0
G, xᵢ
Geometric mean and positive input i.
n, i, Π
Number of inputs, index and product over the inputs.

Example: Preserve the growth product

GEOMETRIC FACTOR
Same question: one constant factor for two equal periods. Apply factor 4 twice to the initial 100 cells. Predicted 1600 = observed 1600. The geometric mean preserves this growth.
\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt{2\times8}=4\\100\times4^2&=1600=100\times2\times8\end{aligned}
G
Equivalent factor 4 per equal period preserves the product 2 × 8.
100, 2
Initial count 100; two equal periods lead to 1600 cells.

Example: Reproduce growth in R

Start with 100 cells and growth factors 2 and 8 over two equal periods.

  • Calculate the geometric factor and use it twice to reconstruct the final count.
factors <- c(2, 8)
g <- prod(factors)^(1 / length(factors))
list(geometric = g, final_cells = 100 * g^length(factors))
c(...)
Combines the two positive growth factors into a vector.
prod(x)
Multiplies the factors to obtain their total multiplier.
length(x)
Counts the factors, here the two equal-duration periods.
list(...)
Returns the geometric factor and reconstructed final count together.

Average on a logarithmic scale

G = \exp\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln x_i\right), \qquad x_i > 0
G, xᵢ
Geometric mean and positive input i.
n, ln, exp
Number of inputs, natural logarithm and inverse exponential.

Example: Two summaries of microbial counts

ARITHMETIC: PULLED UPWARD
10, 100, 10,000 counts per 100 mL The extreme 10,000 strongly raises the mean to 3370. Not a suitable typical value for this log-scale question.
\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{10+100+10000}{3}\\&=3370\end{aligned}
A
Arithmetic mean of the three equally weighted counts.
10, 100, 10000
Illustrative counts per 100 mL; result has the same unit.
GEOMETRIC: LOG-SCALE CENTER
Give equal weight to logarithms of positive counts. 215.44 per 100 mL better describes this log-scale center. Keep the extreme observation; neither center establishes safety.
\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt[3]{10\times100\times10000}\\&\approx215.44\end{aligned}
G, ∛
Geometric mean of three positive counts; ∛ is the cube root.
10, 100, 10000
Illustrative counts per 100 mL; result has the same unit.

Example: Summarize proportional changes

ARITHMETIC: TOO HIGH FOR THIS QUESTION
Three concentration comparisons: 0.5, 2, 5 (dimensionless). 2.5 exceeds the equal-log-weight center 1.710. It does not preserve the product: 2.5³ = 15.625, not 5.
A=(0.5+2+5)/3=2.5
A
Arithmetic mean of three equally weighted ratios.
0.5, 2, 5
Illustrative dimensionless ratios.
GEOMETRIC: PRESERVES THE PRODUCT
The cube root of 5 matches the equal-log-weight question. G³ = 0.5 × 2 × 5 = 5. These are concentration comparisons, not successive growth periods.
G=\sqrt[3]{0.5\times2\times5}\approx1.710
G, ∛
Equivalent factor with equal logarithmic weight; cube root for three inputs.
0.5, 2, 5
Positive dimensionless input ratios.

Example: Two equal distances, two speeds

A tracer travels 100 m at 10 m/s and another 100 m at 2 m/s. What is total distance divided by total time? Compare with the arithmetic average of the speeds.

Example: Which average preserves travel time?

ARITHMETIC CANDIDATE
Equal-distance sections are not equal-time weights. Predicted 33.33 s ≠ actual 60 s.
\begin{aligned}A&=(10+2)/2=6\;\mathrm{m/s}\\t_A&=200/6\approx33.33\;\mathrm{s}\end{aligned}
A
Arithmetic average of the two speeds, in m/s.
t_A, 200 m
Predicted journey time if both 100 m sections were travelled at A.
GEOMETRIC CANDIDATE
A product of speeds answers a different question. Predicted 44.72 s ≠ actual 60 s.
\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt{10\times2}\approx4.472\;\mathrm{m/s}\\t_G&=200/\sqrt{20}\approx44.72\;\mathrm{s}\end{aligned}
G
Geometric average of the two positive speeds, in m/s.
t_G, 200 m
Predicted journey time at constant speed G over the total distance.

harmonic mean

For positive rates over equal quantities, add the corresponding times. Equal times instead imply arithmetic averaging of rates.
H = \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1/x_i}
H, xᵢ
Harmonic mean and nonzero input i; rate examples use positive values.
n, Σ 1/xᵢ
n counts the inputs; add their reciprocals. For speeds in m/s, 1/xᵢ is time per metre (s/m), so H is again in m/s.

Example: Harmonic speed, then total time

\begin{aligned}v_H&=\frac{2}{1/10+1/2}\\&=\frac{10}{3}\;\mathrm{m/s}\\&\approx3.333\;\mathrm{m/s}\end{aligned}
v_H
Harmonic speed in m/s; use exact 10/3 for the next calculation.
2, 10, 2
Two equal 100 m sections; positive speeds 10 and 2 m/s.
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{d}{v_H}\\&=\frac{200}{10/3}\\&=60\;\mathrm{s}\end{aligned}
t
Total journey time in seconds, not one section time.
d, v_H
Total distance 100 + 100 = 200 m; exact speed 10/3 m/s.

Example: Reproduce the journey in R

Travel two equal 100 m sections at 10 and 2 m/s.

  • Calculate section times, total time and overall speed.
  • Check that the harmonic mean gives the same overall speed.
speeds <- c(10, 2)
distances <- rep(100, 2)
times <- distances / speeds
list(times_s = times, total_time_s = sum(times),
     overall_m_s = sum(distances) / sum(times),
     harmonic_m_s = 1 / mean(1 / speeds))
c(...)
Combines the two section speeds into a vector.
rep(x, times)
Repeats 100 m twice to represent equal section distances.
sum(x)
Adds section distances or travel times to their journey totals.
mean(x)
Averages reciprocal speeds; taking its reciprocal gives the harmonic mean.
list(...)
Returns named times and speeds together, with units in their names.

Example: Pump three equal volumes

Pump three successive 10 L batches at 10, 2 and 5 L/min. Calculate each pumping time and the overall rate as total volume divided by total time.

rates <- c(10, 2, 5)
volumes <- rep(10, 3)
times <- volumes / rates
list(times = times,
     overall = sum(volumes) / sum(times),
     harmonic = 1 / mean(1 / rates),
     arithmetic = mean(rates))
c(...)
Combines the three rates into a vector.
rep(x, times)
Repeats a batch volume three times, matching one batch to each rate.
sum(x)
Adds all batch volumes or all pumping times.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean, here for comparison with overall rate.
list(...)
Returns the named times and rates together.

Example: Diffusion through equal layers

Idealized steady-state model: equal thickness and area, layers in series, no reaction or partition discontinuity.
D_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{2}{1/(2\times10^{-6})+1/(10^{-8})}\approx1.99\times10^{-8}\;\mathrm{m^2/s}
Dₑff
Effective diffusion coefficient in m²/s for two equal series layers.
D₁, D₂
2 × 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁸ m²/s; equal thickness/area, steady state, no reaction or partition jump.

Example: One large turbidity measurement

NTU = nephelometric turbidity units (light scattering). The extreme 45.0 NTU strongly pulls the arithmetic mean above the four values around 2.0 to 2.3 NTU. The event is not automatically invalid; keep it visible.
\bar{x}=\frac{53.6}{5}=10.72\;\mathrm{NTU}
x̄
Arithmetic mean of all five values, in NTU.
53.6, 5
Sum 2.1 + 2.3 + 2.0 + 2.2 + 45.0; five equal weights.

median

Sort the sample before choosing its center.
MIDDLE POSITION
At least half of values lie on each side. Odd n: middle observation Even n: average the two middle observations
ORDER, NOT MAGNITUDE
Less sensitive to extreme magnitudes than the mean, not unaffected by every extreme observation. Keep and investigate unusual observations.
\tilde{x}=\begin{cases}x_{((n+1)/2)}, & n\text{ odd}\\\frac{x_{(n/2)}+x_{(n/2+1)}}{2}, & n\text{ even}\end{cases}
x̃
Sample median: the center of the sorted observations.
x₍ⱼ₎, n
Observation at sorted position j; n is the sample size.

Example: Sort first, then find the middle

FIVE VALUES
Sorted: 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 45.0 Middle value: [2.2] NTU Two observations on each side
\tilde{x}=x_{(3)}=2.2\;\mathrm{NTU}
x̃
Median turbidity of five observations, in NTU.
x₍₃₎
Third sorted value: the middle observation 2.2 NTU.
FOUR VALUES
Sorted: 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 Middle pair: [2.1, 2.2] NTU Average these two observations.
\tilde{x}=\frac{2.1+2.2}{2}=2.15\;\mathrm{NTU}
x̃
Median turbidity of four observations, in NTU.
2.1, 2.2
Two middle sorted observations; their mean is 2.15 NTU.

Example: A center does not describe every event

ARITHMETIC MEAN
0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8, 15.0 µg/L Uses the sum of all concentrations.
\bar{x}=3.52\;\mathrm{\mu g/L}
x̄
Arithmetic mean of five equally weighted lead concentrations.
µg/L
Micrograms per litre: result 3.52 µg/L, not a safety threshold.
MEDIAN
Uses the middle sorted observation. Investigate the large observation. Neither center establishes safety.
\tilde{x}=0.7\;\mathrm{\mu g/L}
x̃
Middle sorted lead concentration, not a safety threshold.
µg/L
Micrograms per litre: median 0.7 µg/L.

Example: Find the Pb median in R

Use the same Pb concentrations: 0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8 and 15.0 µg/L.

  • Sort all five observations and calculate their median.
  • Does a small median make the 15.0 µg/L event unimportant?
pb <- c(0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8, 15.0)
list(sorted = sort(pb), median = median(pb))
c(...)
Combines all five Pb concentrations into a vector, including 15.0.
sort(x)
Returns the concentrations in increasing order without discarding any.
median(x)
Returns the sample median: the middle observation here, 0.7 µg/L.
list(...)
Returns the sorted observations and median together so both are visible.

Choose the summary for the question

ARITHMETIC
Repeated measurements · peak areas · intensities · concentrations (same quantity, comparable conditions, equal weights).
GEOMETRIC
Growth factors (equal periods) · positive data spanning orders of magnitude (multiplicative / log-scale center, not range alone; convert % rates to positive factors).
HARMONIC
Speeds (equal distances) · positive quantities averaged via reciprocals (equal-time speed averages are arithmetic).
MEDIAN
Data with extreme values (middle sorted observation; less sensitive to magnitudes, but extreme events remain relevant).

Which summary answers the question?

Equal-weight nitrate replicates are 4.8, 5.0 and 5.2 mg/L. Which center summarizes the additive measurements? State your sampling assumptions.

Comparable, equally weighted sensors report 480, 500 and 520 µS/cm. Calculate an average. What would change if sensor precision or calibration differed?

Three simultaneous phosphorus inputs are 200, 300 and 200 g/s. The question is total input to the lake. Is a mean the quantity you need?

Microplastic counts are 100, 1000 and 10000 particles/kg. Compare an additive average, an equal-log-weight average and a median. Does this dataset alone determine the correct scientific summary?

Pesticide concentrations at three sites are 0.01, 0.1 and 1.0 µg/L. Which question would justify arithmetic, geometric or median summaries? Can three numbers establish a log-normal distribution?

Three reactors in series have rate constants 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 per hour. Is being in series enough to infer a harmonic mean effective rate? What physical model is missing?

Variance and Uncertainty of the Mean

Same Mean, Different Spread

  • Scenario: compare measurement series A and B.
  • Their arithmetic means are the same: 32/3 mg/L.
  • Do they show the same measurement behavior?

Why Does Spread Matter in the Laboratory?

  • Scenario: two analytical methods measure the same control sample.
  • Both give results around the target, with different variability.
  • Would one method be preferable?

Back to Our Three-Observation Example

Scenario: compare individual observations
The two series share the mean 32/3 mg/L. Compare each value with its own series mean. Which signed deviations produce the greater spread?
  • To describe spread, we need to examine the distances between individual observations and their arithmetic mean.

Deviations from the Mean

d_i=x_i-\bar{x}
d_i
Observation minus its sample mean.
i
Observation index (1 to n).
x_i
Individual observed value.
x̄
Arithmetic sample mean.
  • A signed deviation gives direction and distance from the sample mean.

Residuals Share One Exact Constraint

\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0
Why deviations about the arithmetic mean sum to zero
d_i=x_i-\bar{x}

Sum both sides over the observations

\begin{gathered}a_i=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n)\\\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\end{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)
Sum indexed equalities

Add the left sides and the right sides of equalities that hold at every index. This gives a consequence; the summed equality alone does not recover every individual equality.

\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)

For each observation, dᵢ = xᵢ − x̄. Add these equalities for i = 1 through n. The result sums the left-hand residuals and the right-hand deviations. This implication needs no probability assumption. It does not say that one summed equation can recover all individual observations.

n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.

d_i
Observation minus its sample mean.
i
Observation index (1 to n).
n
Number of observations.
x_i
Individual observed value.
x̄
Arithmetic sample mean.
Σ
Sum over the displayed indices.
\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)

Split the sum; count the same mean n times

\begin{aligned}\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-c)&=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-nc\end{aligned}\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x
Split a sum and count the constant

First distribute the sum over a difference. The second sum repeats c exactly n times and equals nc.

\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x

Use aᵢ = xᵢ and c = x̄ in the general rule. Distribute the sum over subtraction. Within this observed sample, the same fitted mean is subtracted at every index. Its sum is n times x̄. The fitted mean may change between samples, but not between indices within one sample.

c has the same value for every index i within the sum; n is a positive integer.

d_i
Observation minus its sample mean.
i
Observation index (1 to n).
n
Number of observations.
x_i
Individual observed value.
x̄
Arithmetic sample mean.
Σ
Sum over the displayed indices.
\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x

Insert the definition of the arithmetic mean

n\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0
Use the arithmetic mean

Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.

\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0

The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their count. Thus n times x̄ is exactly that same sum. Substitute this equality into the difference of sums. A quantity minus itself is zero. This is an exact property of the arithmetic mean, not merely a statement that residuals average to zero across repeated samples.

n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.

d_i
Observation minus its sample mean.
i
Observation index (1 to n).
n
Number of observations.
x_i
Individual observed value.
x̄
Arithmetic sample mean.
Σ
Sum over the displayed indices.
d_i
Observation minus its sample mean.
i
Observation index (1 to n).
n
Number of observations.
Σ
Sum over the displayed indices.
  • Signed deviations from the mean of these same observations sum to zero. Squaring them will retain their size without cancellation.

Squaring the Deviations

\begin{gathered}d_i^2=(x_i-\bar{x})^2\\SS=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i^2\end{gathered}
Square each deviation
xᵢ: observation i; i: index; x̄: sample mean; dᵢ: their signed difference. Superscript 2 denotes squaring.
SS: Sum of Squares
n: observation count; Σ: sum from 1 to n. SS adds the squared deviations. Squaring mg/L produces the unit (mg/L)².
  • Squared deviations do not cancel and therefore preserve information about spread.

Mean Squared Deviation

\mathrm{MSD}=\frac{SS}{n}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n}
Mean squared deviation
MSD: mean squared deviation; SS: sum of squared deviations. xᵢ: observation i; i: index; x̄: sample mean; n: count; Σ: sum from 1 to n.
Squared unit, not absolute distance
The deviations are squared before averaging, so MSD has unit (mg/L)². Division by a count does not change that unit. MSD is not mean absolute distance.
  • MSD describes the average squared deviation per observation.

One Sample from a Hypothetical Lake

Scenario: A fully defined demonstration population of lake concentrations
Population mean: μ = 10 mg/L. Population variance: σ² = 5 (mg/L)². Model: independent normally distributed concentrations. Sample: n = 5, using the existing seed 1904. Goal: compare estimates from one sample with known model parameters.
  • One sample generally does not reproduce the population parameters exactly.
  • One sample cannot establish systematic bias. We need repeated sampling.
  • How does sample size influence the quality of our estimates?

Does the MSD Estimate the True Variance Without Bias?

\mathrm{MSD}_n=\frac1n{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n}(X_i-\bar X)^2

  • Xᵢ and X̄ now vary over hypothetical repeated samples. We ask about the average of the statistic, not just one observed MSD.
  • One MSD may be above or below σ². Systematic underestimation concerns its expectation; simulated averages only approximate that expectation.

Repeated Sampling: Sizes 2 to 100

  • Scenario: a known illustrative normal population, μ = 10 mg/L and σ² = 5 (mg/L)².
  • Draw independent samples of sizes 2–100. How strongly do individual MSD estimates fluctuate?
  • Small samples fluctuate more. Five realizations per size cannot reliably establish bias.

Many Repetitions Check Average Bias

  • For each selected size, simulate 5,000 independent samples and average their MSD estimates.
  • Compare with σ² = 5 (mg/L)². Monte Carlo averages approximate expectations; bias is not the fluctuation of one estimate.
  • Prepared demonstration: average 5,000 independent samples per size, then compare with the known variance.

Where Does the MSD Shortfall Come From?

X_i-\bar X=(X_i-\mu)-(\bar X-\mu)

Square, sum and collect the centered terms

\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-\bar a)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-c)^2\\&\quad-(\bar a-c)^2\end{aligned}\boxed{\begin{aligned}\mathrm{MSD}_n&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}}
Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean

Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.

\boxed{\begin{aligned}\mathrm{MSD}_n&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}}

Centering at the fitted arithmetic mean removes a nonnegative squared shift. The result is an exact identity, not an average statement. Open the full algebra detail for each expansion and summation operation. The population mean is ordinarily unknown; this identity explains the estimator, rather than giving a formula that requires knowing μ.

n is a positive integer, ā = (1/n)Σa_i, and c is fixed with respect to the index. The identity holds deterministically for every finite realization.

Square the centered difference and expand

(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\begin{aligned}(X_i-\bar X)^2&=(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(X_i-\mu)(\bar X-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}
Binomial square

Multiplying a+b by itself gives a², the two equal cross-products ab, and b². Squaring both sides of an equality is a valid implication, not generally a reversible operation without sign information.

\begin{aligned}(X_i-\bar X)^2&=(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(X_i-\mu)(\bar X-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}

Use a = Xᵢ−μ and b = −(X̄−μ) in the binomial identity. Squaring an equality gives a consequence; we do not claim to recover all signs by reversing this step.

\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i+cb_i+q)\\=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i+c\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\\+\sum_{i=1}^n q\end{gathered}\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-\frac2n(\bar X-\mu)\sum_i(X_i-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}
Distribute the sum and factor the cross term

Use linearity for each of the three summands and move the index-independent coefficient c outside the middle sum. The last sum is not simplified yet.

\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-\frac2n(\bar X-\mu)\sum_i(X_i-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}

Distribute the finite sum over the three terms, then divide by the positive n. The same X̄−μ occurs at every index, so it factors out of the cross term. Its squared last term is added n times; the divisor n cancels that count. This is deterministic within each realization.

Variance is an expected squared deviation

For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

\begin{gathered}\operatorname{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2\\\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\end{gathered}

Linearity gives the displayed expectation of the finite squared-distance average; it needs no independence. Each population-centered squared observation has expectation σ². The sample mean has expectation μ under the common-mean condition, so its expected squared shift is Var(X̄). The arithmetic average of n copies of σ² is σ². The complete sample-mean argument is available with the next result.

For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.

Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.

a-\frac an=\frac{n-1}{n}a\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2
Factor a common value

Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.

\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2

In the general factorization use a = σ². The fraction left after subtraction is (n−1)/n, strictly less than one for n > 1. Thus the MSD is biased downward when σ² > 0. A particular realized MSD may lie above or below σ². Bias is the repeated-sampling expectation, not the direction of every individual error.

n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.

E
Repeated-sampling expectation.
MSD_n
Squared residual average, divisor n.
n
Number of observations.
σ²
Population variance.
  • Insert Var(X̄) = σ²/n into E[MSDₙ] = σ² − Var(X̄), then factor the common σ².
  • The downward bias factor is (n−1)/n in expectation, not in every sample. The model assumptions of the preceding result still apply.

Bessel's Correction Removes the Systematic Bias

\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2

Multiply by the reciprocal bias factor, for n > 1

\operatorname{E}[cY]=c\operatorname{E}[Y]\begin{gathered}S^2:=\frac{n}{n-1}\mathrm{MSD}_n\\\boxed{\operatorname{E}[S^2]=\sigma^2}\end{gathered}
Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.

\operatorname{E}[S^2]=\frac{n}{n-1}\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n}{n-1}\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2=\sigma^2

Define the random statistic S² by multiplying MSDₙ by the fixed reciprocal n/(n−1). Linearity moves that coefficient outside E and the factors cancel. S² is unbiased under the stated assumptions. Its observed value s² is not generally exactly σ², and the square root is not automatically unbiased.

For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.

The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.

n > 1, so n−1 is positive and division by n−1 is valid.

Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.

  • S² denotes the statistic across samples; s² is its observed value. The practical formula needs only xᵢ, x̄ and n > 1, not the unknown μ or σ².
  • Unbiasedness means the correct average over hypothetical samples. One realized s² need not equal the population variance.

Theory Explains the Monte Carlo Shortfall

  • Theory explains average bias. Monte Carlo means approximate the curve; they need not lie exactly on it.

Bessel's Correction: Worked Example

From Variance to Standard Deviation

s_A^2=\frac{13}{3}\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2

Take the nonnegative square root

s=\sqrt{s^2}s_A=\sqrt{\frac{13}{3}}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.082\;\mathrm{mg/L}
Definition of standard deviation

Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. Taking the square root also restores the original physical unit. It is not the mean absolute deviation, and an unbiased variance estimate does not imply an unbiased square root.

s_A=\sqrt{\frac{13}{3}}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.082\;\mathrm{mg/L}

Series A has sample variance 13/3 (mg/L)². Take its nonnegative square root: √(13/3) ≈ 2.081666, reported here as 2.082 mg/L. The concentration unit is no longer squared. This is a root-mean-square measure of residual size with the stated divisor, not an arithmetic mean of absolute distances.

What Does SD Tell Us About Precision?

  • Scenario: control sample, assigned reference 10 mg/L. Five determinations per method in one session, with fixed procedure, operator and instrument.
  • Precision is closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions.
  • A has smaller observed SD: closer agreement in this session, not proof of general method suitability.
  • Precision describes agreement under stated measurement conditions.

Repeatability and Measurement Conditions

Repeatability
Scenario: repeat a control measurement within one short run. **Same laboratory and method.** Relevant conditions remain the same over a ==short interval==. Describe which operations were actually repeated.
Intermediate precision
Scenario: compare control results collected on different days. **Same laboratory**, with specified changes. Vary day, operator or instrument deliberately. The design determines which sources are represented.
Reproducibility
Scenario: a defined interlaboratory comparison. **Different laboratories**, under stated conditions. Specify the method, materials and comparison protocol. No universal quantitative ranking follows without data.
  • Choose and report the measurement conditions before interpreting an SD.

Precision, Trueness and Bias

Precision
Scenario: repeat the same control measurement. **Precision** concerns agreement among repeated results. State the measurement conditions and independent units. Small spread does ==not establish trueness==.
Trueness
Scenario: compare an average with a suitable reference. **Trueness** concerns agreement of the long-run average with the reference. A small observed SD does not answer that question. Finite data only estimate the long-run behavior.
Bias
Scenario: a tightly grouped series is centered above the reference. **Bias** is the difference between the expected result and the reference. An observed mean difference estimates bias with uncertainty. A series can be precise and systematically shifted.

Why Precision Alone Is Not Enough

Scenario: same spread, different center
• Compare two series with reference **10 mg/L**. • Their observed **SDs agree**, but their means are **10 and 11 mg/L**. • Does ==precision alone== identify agreement with the reference?
  • A small SD alone does not establish closeness to the reference or method suitability.

What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

Three injections from one vial
Scenario: inject the same prepared material three times. Repeat **injection and detection**; vial, preparation and field sample remain shared. Instrumental variation can become visible. These technical repeats are ==not three independent field units==; drift can also correlate them.
Three independent preparations
Scenario: prepare three separate aliquots of one sample. Repeat **preparation and measurement**; the field sample remains shared. Preparation plus downstream variation can become visible. Independent preparation errors need justification; these are not three independent field samples.
Three independently collected field samples
Scenario: collect, prepare and measure three field samples separately. Repeat **collection and downstream operations**; site or time may remain shared. Field-sampling and analytical variation can both appear. Independence depends on collection design; treating nested readings as independent is pseudoreplication.
  • Measurement repetitions are not automatically independent experimental units.

Sources of Analytical Variation

  • An analytical result may be influenced by several sources of variability.

Combining Variance Contributions

\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=\operatorname{Var}(A+B+C)

Add the independent component variances

\begin{gathered}\operatorname{Var}(A+B)=\operatorname{Var}(A)+\operatorname{Var}(B)\\\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\end{gathered}\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2
Variance of independent additive contributions

For independent finite-variance contributions, covariance terms vanish. Therefore Var(A+B) = Var(A)+Var(B), and the finite-sum extension gives total variance as the sum of component variances. For correlated sources Var(A+B) also contains 2 Cov(A,B). This law concerns an assumed model, not differences between pooled experimental SDs.

\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2

Treat A, B and C as additive random contributions, all expressed in mg/L. Their illustrative variances are 4, 1 and 0.25 (mg/L)². Independence removes the covariance terms. Add the three variances to obtain 5.25 (mg/L)². The numbers are model inputs for teaching, not variance components isolated from the lake or QC data.

Illustrative model, not estimated components: sampling variance 4, preparation variance 1, instrument variance 0.25 (mg/L)². Assume independent additive contributions with finite variance. Correlated sources require covariance terms.

A
Additive sampling contribution in the illustrative model.
B
Additive preparation contribution in the illustrative model.
C
Additive instrument contribution in the illustrative model.
Var
Variance of a random quantity.
σ²total
Total variance in (mg/L)².

From Total Variance to Total SD

\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2

Take one square root after adding

\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{\sum_k\sigma_k^2}\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{5.25}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.291\;\mathrm{mg/L}
Take the square root of total variance

After adding variances in the same squared unit, take one nonnegative square root. Standard deviations are not directly additive. This root-sum-of-squares calculation needs the independence/additivity assumptions used in the preceding step.

\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{5.25}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.291\;\mathrm{mg/L}

Take one square root of the total 5.25 (mg/L)², giving approximately 2.291 mg/L. Adding the individual SDs would give 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 3.5 mg/L, which is not the SD of this independent sum. If contributions were correlated, include covariance terms before taking the square root.

Illustrative model, not estimated components: sampling variance 4, preparation variance 1, instrument variance 0.25 (mg/L)². Assume independent additive contributions with finite variance. Correlated sources require covariance terms.

σtotal
Total standard deviation in mg/L.
σ²total
Total variance in (mg/L)².
√
Nonnegative square root.

What Must We Replicate?

  • Each child belongs to one parent: injections within preparations, preparations within field samples, samples within sites. 81 readings are only three sites, not 81 independent sites.
  • Pooled SDs do not isolate variance components. Replication at the relevant levels plus a suitable hierarchical model may be needed to separate sources.

Lake Sampling: Variation Between Sites

  • Within-site spread and differences between site means are different comparisons.
  • Three values per site cannot separate sampling, preparation and instrument causes without a suitable design.

Relative Standard Deviation

\mathrm{RSD}=\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|},\qquad\mathrm{RSD}(\%)=100\,\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|}
Spread relative to level
RSD: relative standard deviation; s: sample SD; x̄: sample mean. | | takes its absolute value. The mean must be nonzero and sufficiently far from zero.
Ratio or percentage
The units cancel. RSD is dimensionless. Multiplying by 100 expresses its numerical percentage; % denotes percent. A ratio of 0.02 is 2%.
Meaningful ratios
Use a suitable ratio-scale quantity with a meaningful zero and compatible measurement conditions. A nonzero mean alone is not sufficient.

RSD in Analytical Quality Control

  • SD carries the concentration unit. Convert units before comparing absolute SD values: 0.00100747 g/L = 1.00747 mg/L.
  • RSD is dimensionless (reported as %). Multiplying both the mean and SD by the same positive unit factor leaves RSD unchanged.

When RSD Becomes Misleading

  • RSD is undefined at a zero mean and unstable near zero. Blank measurements need absolute-spread assessment.
  • Ratios need a meaningful zero. RSD of Celsius temperatures is inappropriate.

The Influence of an Extreme Measurement

Scenario: change one QC measurement
• Start with **five QC A measurements**. • Replace only ==10.2 by 15.2 mg/L==. • Compare the **mean and spread** before and after.
  • Replace only QC A's 10.2 with 15.2 mg/L. The mean, variance and SD all increase.
  • Investigate the cause. A large effect on the summaries is not a reason for automatic deletion.

R Practice: Evaluate Two QC Methods

  • Compare A/B: means, SDs and RSDs.
  • Count: comparisons return TRUE/FALSE; sum() counts TRUE.
  • Read output: means, SDs, RSD (%) and counts; each in A/B order.
  • Interpret: [9.5, 10.5] mg/L includes endpoints and is ==illustrative, not a validated requirement==.
a <- c(9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.2)
b <- c(8.7, 10.8, 9.5, 11.2, 9.8)
ma <- mean(a); mb <- mean(b)
sa <- sd(a); sb <- sd(b)
ra <- 100*sa/ma; rb <- 100*sb/mb
inside_a <- a >= 9.5 & a <= 10.5
inside_b <- b >= 9.5 & b <= 10.5
na <- sum(inside_a); nb <- sum(inside_b)
c(ma, mb, sa, sb, ra, rb, na, nb)
c(...)
Combines input values or collects output results into a vector.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of x.
sd(x)
Calculates sample SD using the corrected variance.
sum(x)
Adds values; for logical x, counts TRUE entries.
>=, <= and &
Operators: compare to inclusive bounds; & requires both conditions.

Return to the Variance of the Sample Mean

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}
Variance of the sample mean: full derivation
\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i

Apply expectation to the mean's defining equality

U=V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{E}[U]=\operatorname{E}[V]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]
Expectation preserves equality

If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.

\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]

Start from the random sample mean, a fixed-size average of the Xᵢ. Equal integrable random quantities have equal expectations. Independence is not needed for this operation.

For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.

The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.

If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.

Identical sampling supplies E[Xᵢ] = μ at each index. The numerator is nμ, and division by n gives μ. This establishes the equality of theoretical expectations, not equality of each realized x̄ with μ.

s
sample standard deviation
  • **Notation:** Yᵢ names the same measurement variable as before; its mean is Ȳ. **SD** describes individual values; **SE** describes the mean.
  • Variance can describe data or quantify uncertainty of an estimator, including later model parameters. ==s/√n applies to this mean, not every estimator==. Correlation and systematic effects need separate treatment.

Standard Error Decreases as 1/√n

\begin{gathered}\operatorname{SE}_n=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\quad\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0\\\operatorname{SE}_{4n}=\frac12\operatorname{SE}_n\end{gathered}
SE
SD of the mean across repeated samples.
n
Number of observations.
σ
population standard deviation
  • **Square-root law:** at fixed population spread, four times as many independent observations halve the SE. Individual measurement spread does not shrink.
  • **Scope:** independent observations with common finite variance. Correlation or systematic bias can leave ==uncertainty that averaging does not remove==.

Report a Mean with Its Estimated Standard Error

\begin{gathered}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar Y)=\frac{0.1581}{\sqrt5}\approx0.0707\;\mathrm{mg/L}\\\boxed{\bar y\;\pm\;\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar Y)=(10.00\pm0.07)\;\mathrm{mg/L}}\end{gathered}
Ȳ
Random mean of the same measurements, now named Yᵢ.
estimated SE
Estimated SE, using sample SD s.
ȳ
Observed sample mean in the Y notation.
  • **Existing QC A:** 9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.2 mg/L. Assuming iid repeats: n = 5, mean = 10.00 mg/L, s ≈ 0.158 mg/L.
  • **Label error bars:** here ± means ==one estimated SE==, not SD or a 95% confidence interval. It describes random repeatability uncertainty, not all measurement-uncertainty contributions.

What Have We Learned?

  • A common mean can hide different observed spreads.
  • MSD describes data; sample variance estimates population variance under assumptions.
  • Fitting the mean constrains residuals, not the original sampling design.
  • SD has the original unit; RSD expresses spread relative to the mean magnitude.
  • Precision and analytical decisions require stated measurement conditions.

A report says ‘10.0 ± 0.2 mg/L’. What does ± denote? Which sample size, independent units and measurement conditions must be stated before you can interpret it?

Same mean. Same variance. Same distribution?

Scenario: identical summaries
• Four synthetic sets, **100 values each**. • All have the **same mean and sample SD**. • Do they also have the ==same distribution==?
  • **Equal mean and SD do not determine the empirical distribution.**
  • Beyond mean and SD: ECDF, quantiles and distribution shape.

A dataset starts with a measurement question

Five repeated nitrate determinations of one prepared water sample; acquisition order, values in mg/L.
\begin{gathered}x_1,\ldots,x_n,\qquad n=5\\(10.2,\ 9.8,\ 10.0,\ 10.0,\ 10.1)\;\mathrm{mg/L}\end{gathered}
What does i identify?
i labels the observation in acquisition order, not its rank. n counts all readings, including ties. Synthetic teaching data.
  • Repeat determinations describe this preparation, **not variability between water samples**.
  • Retain sample identity, unit and acquisition order alongside every value.

Parentheses turn an index into a rank

Sort the same five observations from smallest to largest. No measurement is removed or changed; equal values keep separate ranks.
\begin{gathered}(x_1,\ldots,x_5)=(10.2,9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1)\\x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(5)}\\(x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(5)})=(9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1,10.2)\end{gathered}
Same values, different meaning of the index
All values are in mg/L. x₁=10.2, but x₍₁₎=9.8 is the minimum. x₍₂₎=x₍₃₎=10.0: two observations, not one. x₍ₙ₎ is the maximum.
  • **i: observation identity. (i): rank after sorting.** Parentheses are not optional.
  • Sorted values alone cannot reveal acquisition order or a time trend.

Range: the span of the observations

For a nonempty finite sample, range is maximum minus minimum, in the original measurement unit. It describes only the extrema.
R=x_{(n)}-x_{(1)},\qquad n\ge1
Order first
x₍₁₎ is the minimum; x₍ₙ₎ is the maximum. R is a width, not the endpoint pair returned by R's range(x).
  • **Only the extrema matter**, not the arrangement between them.
  • One extreme value can change it strongly. Consider sample size and context.

Range: repeat measurements or different samples?

Two uses: different measurement questions
• **Repeat:** what span did 50 nitrate determinations of one preparation cover? • **River:** what concentrations did 50 different grab samples cover? • Synthetic teaching data; both in mg/L.
  • Use range for the **observed span**. The river span is not repeatability; neither span is a validated working range.

Range: the same span can hide different data

Counterexample: two concentration profiles
• Same n=5, minimum 0 and maximum 10 mg/L. • **Centre-heavy:** most values near 5. • **Endpoint-heavy:** most values at 0 or 10. • Constructed synthetic profiles, not instrument trials.
  • **Range misses the interior.** Compare all observations, not endpoints alone.
  • More observations offer more chances for extremes: report n when comparing spans.

Quartiles: three landmarks in ordered data

The first, second and third quartiles correspond to p=0.25, 0.50 and 0.75; computed sample quartiles require the same explicitly chosen quantile convention.
Q_1=\widehat Q(0.25),\quad Q_2=\widehat Q(0.50),\quad Q_3=\widehat Q(0.75)
Quarter, half, three quarters
Q₁, Q₂ and Q₃ are the lower quartile, sample median and upper quartile. Q̂(p) is the linearly interpolated sample quantile at cumulative proportion p. The fractions 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 are unitless; all quantile values have the measurement unit.
  • Quartiles locate positions in ordered data; they are **not distances**.
  • **Ties and interpolation:** the four parts need not contain exactly 25% each.

Quartiles: locate the typical concentration levels

Two uses for nitrate summaries
• **River survey:** locate the middle and outer quartiles of the sampled concentrations. • **Effluent:** summarize central observed levels without reducing everything to the mean. • Synthetic samples, **n=50 each**; linear interpolation.
  • Quartiles describe **levels**, not just widths. These synthetic summaries do not establish compliance or treatment effectiveness.

Quartiles: a high concentration can disappear

Counterexample: do quartiles catch a high sample?
• **50 synthetic river concentrations**, 0.5 to 25 mg/L. • Replace the maximum **25 by 90 mg/L**; retain the other 49 values. • Same linearly interpolated quartiles, very different maximum. • Constructed comparison, not paired field evidence.
  • **Always inspect the tail.** Matching quartiles neither rule out high concentrations nor justify discarding them.

Quantiles: choose any probability

A value calculated from observed data at probability p using a declared quantile method; it can describe the sample or estimate a population quantile under sampling assumptions.
\begin{gathered}h=1+(n-1)p,\quad j=\lfloor h\rfloor,\quad d=h-j\\\widehat Q(p)=(1-d)x_{(j)}+d\,x_{(j+1)}\\ n\ge2,\quad 0\le p<1\end{gathered}
Interpolate between adjacent ranks
p: unitless cumulative proportion; n: number of observations; h: fractional rank; floor(h): round h down to integer j; d: unitless interpolation weight h−j. x₍ⱼ₎ and x₍ⱼ₊₁₎ are adjacent ordered values; Q̂(p) is their weighted average, in the measurement unit. The factors 1−d and d sum to one. The displayed interior case requires n≥2 and p<1; at p=1 return the maximum, and for n=1 return the sole observation.
  • The 90th percentile uses **p=0.90**, not p=90. Quartiles are special quantiles.
  • Declare the method: interpolated quantiles need not be observed values.

Quantiles: ask specifically about the upper tail

Two descriptive uses: choose p to match the question
• **River:** describe the upper observed concentration region with p=0.90. • **Blank:** summarize high blank-equivalent signals with p=0.90. • Synthetic uncensored readings; **n=50 each**, linear interpolation.
  • The interpolated 90th percentile need not be measured. Here h=45.1: **0.9 × rank 45 + 0.1 × rank 46**.

Quantiles: five blanks cannot define a detection limit

Counterexample: estimate a high tail from n=5
• Compare **0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4** with **0,0.1,0.2,0.3,2.0 mg/L**. • At p=0.95, linear interpolation puts **80% weight on the maximum**. • Both are synthetic blank-equivalent series.
  • A high quantile from a tiny sample is **tail-sensitive**, not a well-established population threshold.
  • A descriptive blank quantile alone is **not an analytical detection limit**; validation and error probabilities need a separate design.

IQR: the distance between the outer quartiles

The upper quartile minus the lower quartile, using one consistent quantile convention. The linked expression defines the descriptive sample IQR using linearly interpolated quantiles, whereas Tukey boxplot hinges may differ.
\mathrm{IQR}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\widehat Q(0.75)-\widehat Q(0.25),\quad n\ge1
A width in the original unit
x₁,…,xₙ: observed values; n≥1: sample size. Q̂(p): linearly interpolated sample quantile at unitless proportion p. Subtract the lower quartile at 0.25 from the upper quartile at 0.75. IQR is this central width in the measurement unit, not the entire observed range.
  • Less sensitive to some tail changes than range or SD; **not immune**.
  • Same unit as SD, but not interchangeable with it or a confidence interval.

IQR: compare the central spread of recoveries

Two uses at the same fortification level
• **Extraction A vs B:** which has less central recovery spread? • **Control series:** summarize central variation over 50 runs. • Synthetic recoveries (%), **n=50 each**; linear interpolation.
  • A has a smaller IQR here. For the control series, **also inspect run order**: a narrow spread does not establish stability.

IQR: a narrow band can still miss the target

Counterexample: same spread, shifted recovery
• Nominal control target: **100%**. • Two synthetic series, **n=50 each**. • Medians **100% versus 110%**. • Both IQRs are **1.96 percentage points**.
  • **Spread is not trueness.** Report location relative to the target as well; do not choose a method by IQR alone.

MAD: a median of absolute deviations

The median of the absolute differences between observations and their sample median; the raw statistic is not automatically scaled to estimate standard deviation.
\mathrm{MAD}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathrm{median}_i\left|x_i-\mathrm{median}_j(x_j)\right|
Two median operations
First find the sample median; then find the median of all absolute distances to it. No squaring and no averaging of these distances.
  • R: **mad(x, constant=1)** is raw; the default scales by **1.4826**.
  • Ties can make raw MAD zero even when observations are not all equal.

MAD: describe typical departures, retain unusual readings

Two questions for repeated nitrate determinations
• **Repeat:** typical departure from the median in 50 determinations. • **High reading:** describe central scatter while investigating one unusual result. • Synthetic series, **n=50 each**; raw MAD, mg/L.
  • Raw MAD changes only **0.25 → 0.26 mg/L** here. Retain and investigate 15 mg/L: robust does not mean unchanged.

MAD: zero does not mean perfect repeatability

Counterexample: coarse reporting creates ties
• Synthetic readings rounded to whole mg/L: **10,10,10,10,11**. • Median 10; ordered absolute deviations **0,0,0,0,1**. • The middle deviation is zero, but the range is 1 mg/L.
  • Check **measurement/reporting resolution**. MAD=0 is not proof of zero underlying variation.
  • In R use **constant=1** for raw MAD; the default 1.4826 scaling cannot undo rounding.

SD, IQR and MAD: three different questions

**Control-signal repeatability** 100 synthetic normal-like readings; mean **50**, sample SD **10 a.u.** Same observations in each column.
**Choose the question** - **SD:** repeatability and variance-based models; sensitive to extremes. - **IQR:** middle-rank width for skewed data/boxplots; ignores tail magnitude. - **Raw MAD:** robust median distance; may be zero with ties.
**Different interval choices** Mean ± SD; [Q₁,Q₃]; median ± raw MAD. **IQR = Q₃−Q₁ is a width, not a radius.** Quartiles use linear interpolation; MAD constant 1. ==Actual closed-interval coverage, not confidence intervals or universal percentages.==

Same SD, different coverage: a long upper tail

**Scenario: occasional high detector responses** 100 synthetic right-skewed readings. Mean **50** and sample SD **10 a.u.**, just as before; median **46.919**.
**Read the consequences** - Mean ± SD: **85/100** readings, not 68. - IQR **11.024 a.u.** describes the middle ranks. - Raw MAD **4.900 a.u.** describes a typical median distance. - The quartile interval is **not centred on the median**.
**Application and limit** Use median/IQR or MAD when tail values dominate a mean-based summary. But retain the tail for exposure or contamination questions. ==Robust does not mean scientifically unimportant extremes may be ignored.==

Boxplots: construct and read the summary

Construction: declare the convention first
Reference: **2,4,4,5,5,6,7 mg/L**. - **Quartiles:** use linear interpolation. - **Fences:** Q₁−1.5 IQR and Q₃+1.5 IQR. - **Whiskers:** last observed values inside. ==Whiskers end at observations, not fences.==
  • Read **median → quartile box → whiskers → flagged points**. Box length shows IQR, not SD.
  • A boxplot does **not reveal modality**, sample size or every observation. Base R Tukey hinges can differ from ggplot2 quartiles.

Boxplots: compare methods and sample matrices

Two comparisons: same fortification level
**50 synthetic preparations per group**; recoveries (%), linearly interpolated quartiles. - **Method:** extraction A versus B in matrix 1. - **Matrix:** extraction A in matrices 1 versus 2. ==Same fortification level in both comparisons.==
  • Compare **median and IQR together**. The matrix-2 shift motivates investigation; these small groups do not prove a causal matrix effect.

Boxplots: identical boxes can hide a run-order trend

Counterexample: keep the chronological sequence
Synthetic control-sample runs: **the same five values**. - **Increasing:** 98,99,100,101,102%. - **Reordered:** 100,98,102,99,101%. ==Same boxplot, different run order.== Only the first sequence is strictly increasing.
  • A boxplot **discards time order**. Add a run chart before judging drift or stability; five runs alone do not establish a process model.

Boxplots: extreme observations are separate points

**50 synthetic river concentrations**: one at **90 mg/L**, the other 49 at 0.5–24.5 mg/L.
Read the summary (mg/L): - **Quartiles:** Q₁ 6.625, median 12.75, Q₃ 18.875. - **Upper fence:** 37.25. - **Upper whisker:** 24.5, not 37.25 or 90.
==Flagged does not mean diagnosed.== Before interpreting **90 mg/L**, check: - Sample identity and sampling records. - Instrument records.

Boxplots: a roughly symmetric central pattern

**100 synthetic detector responses**; not a fitted population model.
Read the central pattern: - **Median:** 50 a.u., near the box centre. - **Quartiles:** about 43.32 and 56.68 a.u. Comparable halves and whiskers are consistent with **central symmetry**.
==Not a normality test.== Inspect the **small raw points**: they reveal tail detail that the box suppresses.

Boxplots: a longer upper tail

**100 synthetic right-skewed responses**, standardized to mean **50** and sample SD **10 a.u.**
Read the asymmetry: - **Median:** 46.92 a.u. - **Quartiles:** about 42.84 and 53.86 a.u. The **upper box half and upper tail** are longer.
==Large values are not automatically errors.== They may be expected **tail observations**. The boxplot suggests asymmetry, but does not identify its cause.

Boxplots: two clusters can disappear inside one box

**100 synthetic detector responses** from two constructed clusters.
Read the gap: - **Median:** 50 a.u., between the clusters. - **Quartiles:** Q₁ about 40.22, Q₃ about 59.78 a.u. The box spans a **sparsely occupied region**.
==One box can hide two modes.== - **Raw points** reveal the gap. - Check a **histogram** before calling the centre typical.

Boxplots: symmetry does not imply a bell shape

**100 evenly spaced synthetic responses**. Mean **50** and sample SD **10 a.u.** match the preceding examples.
Read the symmetric box: - **Median:** 50 a.u. - **Quartiles:** about 41.47 and 58.53 a.u. Here it comes from **nearly flat occupancy**, not a bell-shaped sample.
==Similar boxes do not imply similar distributions.== Boxplots summarize **ranks**. Inspect the observations and binning-based views as well.

R lab: build and inspect a ggplot2 boxplot

Synthetic recoveries: 50 preparations per group.

  • Run: compare methods, then matrices. Inspect ggplot_build().
  • Change: the final 110 to 140. Predict box, whisker and flag first.
  • Explain: why does the box stay unchanged?

==A fence is not a whisker endpoint.== Flags do not remove observations.

May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  if (requireNamespace("webr", quietly = TRUE)) webr::install("ggplot2")
  else stop("Install ggplot2 first: install.packages('ggplot2')")
}
library(ggplot2)
groups <- c("A / matrix 1", "B / matrix 1", "A / matrix 2")
d <- data.frame(series = rep(groups, each = 50),
  value = c(seq(95.1, by=0.2, length.out=50),
            seq(80.4, by=0.8, length.out=50),
            seq(70.8, by=0.8, length.out=50)))
d$value[150] <- 110
d$series <- factor(d$series, levels = groups)
p <- ggplot(d, aes(series, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(coef = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Synthetic extraction / matrix", y = "Recovery (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
print(p)
ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]][c("lower", "middle", "upper", "ymin", "ymax", "outliers")]
ggplot() + aes()
Map the extraction/matrix group to x and recovery (%) to y.
geom_boxplot(coef=1.5)
Use ggplot2's usual linearly interpolated quartiles and 1.5×IQR fences; flag rather than remove distant values.
ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]]
Inspect the computed quartiles, whisker endpoints and separately plotted observations.
c(...)
**Combine** values or output-column names into a vector; does not sort them.
data.frame(...)
Build a table with one row per synthetic observation and named series/value columns.
seq(...)
Generate a synthetic grid: **by** sets its increment; **length.out** sets the number of values.
rep(groups, each=50)
Repeat every group label **50 times**, aligning labels with the synthetic observations.
factor(..., levels=groups)
Declare categories and their display order; the recovery values do not change.
requireNamespace(..., quietly=TRUE)
Check package availability without attaching it. TRUE/FALSE selects the setup branch.
webr::install("ggplot2")
Download ggplot2 into browser R if missing. **Network required**; learner observations are not uploaded.
stop(...)
Stop with a setup error. Desktop R needs ggplot2 installed separately.
library(ggplot2)
Attach the installed package so its functions can be called by name.
print(p)
Draw the ggplot object explicitly in the browser R runtime.
labs(x=..., y=...)
Label axes, including the **recovery unit (%)**.
theme_minimal(base_size=16)
Set the plot theme and base font size; **appearance only**, not a statistical calculation.
<-, $, [, [[, +, if / else, ! and ::
**<-** assigns; **$** selects a column; **[** subsets; **[[** extracts a list element. **+** adds ggplot layers; **if/else** branches; **!** negates; **::** selects a package function.

Histograms: each bar represents a bin

**Question** How are 100 numerical readings distributed? Group adjacent values into **equal-width bins**, not unrelated categories.
**Read the bars** - Width: **5 a.u. per bin**. - Height: **observations in that interval**. - A bar is not one observation or the measured signal height.
**Check the boundaries** Intervals are [left,right); the last includes its right edge. ==Every observation is counted exactly once.==

Read a histogram: centre, spread and occupancy

**Scenario** 100 synthetic responses from repeated measurements of a control signal.
**Interpretation** - Centre near **50 a.u.** - Fewer observations in either tail. - Read **location, spread and symmetry together**.
**Limit** ==Taller means more observations in this interval==, not higher concentration or proof of a population distribution.

Read a histogram: a long right tail

**Scenario** Many moderate synthetic responses, a few much larger ones.
**Interpretation** - Bulk near the lower end. - **Long right tail**. - Mean **50** exceeds median **46.92 a.u.**
**Investigate, do not diagnose** Sampling, mixtures or contamination may matter. ==A tail value is not automatically an error.== Time order is absent.

Read a histogram: two occupied regions

**Scenario** 100 synthetic detector responses from two narrow groups.
**Interpretation** - Peaks near **40 and 60 a.u.** - Few observations near **50**. - One centre may sit in a gap.
**Next question** Check **matrix, batch or method labels**. The plot suggests subgroups; it does not identify their cause or significance.

2D histograms: bin paired measurements on two axes

**Scenario: paired measurements** 60 concentration/response pairs. Keep each pair together and count observations in rectangular cells.
**Read a cell** - Intersection of an **x bin and a y bin**. - Number and color encode **count**. - Empty cell: **zero** observations.
**Do not confuse the encodings** Equal widths within each axis. ==Color is frequency, not response magnitude.== Read both axes and the count scale.

Read a 2D histogram: an upward band, not a calibration

**Scenario** The same 60 synthetic paired sensor readings, aggregated on a concentration–response grid.
**Interpretation** Occupied cells form an **upward band**: higher concentrations tend to accompany higher responses here.
**Limit** Binning hides exact pairs and within-cell scatter. ==Not a fitted calibration==, proof of linearity or a causal conclusion.

Bin width too large: the structure is averaged away

**One change** Same two-cluster data; now **one bin from 30 to 70 a.u.**
**What survives?** - Count: **100**. - Gap and two occupied regions: **hidden**.
**Verdict for this question** ==Too coarse.== A correct count can still be an unhelpful view.

Bin width too small: occupancy becomes fragmented

**One change** Same 100 responses; **400 bins**, width **0.1 a.u.**
**What dominates?** - Most counts: **0 or 1**. - Individual gaps and spikes. - Not hundreds of demonstrated subpopulations.
**Verdict for this question** Too little aggregation. ==More bins is not automatically more information.==

A useful resolution: compare the same data again

**One change** Same 100 responses; **ten bins of width 4 a.u.**, spanning 30–70 a.u.
**What can we see now?** - Two occupied regions. - A **sparse middle**. - Aggregation beyond individual spikes.
**Still check alternatives** Useful here, not universally optimal. Compare **neighboring widths** and the instrument's resolution.

Bin origin matters as well as width

**One change** Width stays **4 a.u.**; move the first edge **30 → 32**. All 100 responses remain covered.
**Watch the boundaries** Some observations enter different bins and heights change. ==No measured value changed.==
**Comparison rule** Trust features that survive reasonable changes. Compare groups with **common edges and compatible normalization**.

Bin rules are starting points

Freedman–Diaconis (FD) uses IQR, Scott's rule uses SD, and Sturges' rule suggests a bin count.
\begin{gathered}h_{FD}=2\,\mathrm{IQR}\,n^{-1/3}\\h_{Scott}=3.5\,s\,n^{-1/3}\\k_{Sturges}=\lceil1+\log_2 n\rceil\end{gathered}
Names and symbols
FD = Freedman–Diaconis; Scott = Scott's rule; Sturges = Sturges' rule. h: width; k: bin count; n: observations; s: sample SD. IQR uses linear interpolation.
  • For h>0 start with **ceil((max−min)/h)** bins; convenient-edge rounding can change that count.
  • **IQR=0 gives FD width 0.** Handle ties/constant data explicitly; no rule is universally best.

Apply a rule, then inspect neighboring choices

**Explore the same 100 readings** Sample SD **10**, linearly interpolated IQR **13.35**, observed span **51.59 a.u.** Change width and origin on the right.
**Starting rules** - **Freedman–Diaconis:** width ≈5.75. - **Scott:** width ≈7.54. - **Sturges:** 8 bins over the observed span.
**Try it** Choose a rule, move the sliders, then **Reset bins**. The covering grid may add a boundary bin. ==The count must stay 100.==

Unequal bins: compare areas

Equal widths are optional. Adaptive bins can be narrow in dense regions and wide in sparse tails.
\begin{gathered}h_j=b_{j+1}-b_j\\d_j=\frac{n_j}{n\,h_j}\\d_jh_j=\frac{n_j}{n},\qquad\sum_j d_jh_j=1\end{gathered}
Reading the symbols
b: edges; hⱼ: bin width; nⱼ: count; n: total. Density has inverse measurement units; bar area is the sample fraction.
  • Raw count heights would visually reward wide bins. Use **count / (n × bin width)** for relative-frequency density.
  • The area of each bar is its sample fraction; total area is **1**. Density can exceed 1 without representing a probability above 100%.

Unequal bins, step 1: sort and choose ranks

**Small calculation, not an application-sized dataset** Eight constructed concentrations: **1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20 mg/L**. We want four bins following the occupied ranks, rather than equal measurement widths. - Choose boundaries at **minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃, maximum**. - For linear interpolation, h = 1 + (n−1)p. Here n = 8. - Interpolate between the observations at ranks floor(h) and floor(h)+1. ==This is one data-dependent choice, not a unique correct partition.==

Step 2: calculate the actual edges

**Use n = 8 and x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20** - p = .25: h = **2.75** → Q₁ = 2 + .75(3−2) = **2.75**. - p = .50: h = **4.5** → median = 4 + .5(5−4) = **4.5**. - p = .75: h = **6.25** → Q₃ = 6 + .25(10−6) = **7**. Edges: **1, 2.75, 4.5, 7, 20 mg/L**. Widths: **1.75, 1.75, 2.5, 13 mg/L**. **Count once:** [1,2.75), [2.75,4.5), [4.5,7), [7,20]. Each contains two observations. With ties, equal counts are not guaranteed; merge repeated boundaries.

Step 3: heights must preserve area

**Same count, unequal width** Each bin contains **2/8 = 25%** of the observations. Density height = count / (n × width). - First two bins: .25/1.75 = **1/7 ≈ .14286**. - Third: .25/2.5 = **.10**. - Last: .25/13 = **1/52 ≈ .01923** (mg/L)⁻¹. ==Height × width = .25 for every bar; total area = 1.== The tall first bar does not contain more observations than the wide last bar.

Construct adaptive bins with quantile boundaries

**Return to 100 readings** After the worked construction, use min, linearly interpolated Q₁, median, Q₃ and max as adaptive boundaries.
**Edges and occupancy** - Edges ≈**39.93, 42.84, 46.92, 53.86, 93.69**. - **25 observations per bin**. - Different widths, different heights.
**Area check** ==Each area is 25%.== Height is 0.25/width. Merge repeated quantile edges instead of creating zero-width bins.

Adaptive bins: resolve the bulk without overstating the tail

**Application** Resolve a dense low-response region while summarizing a sparse long upper tail.
**Benefit** - Narrow bins near the bulk. - Fewer almost-empty tail bins. - The low last bar still has **25% area**.
**Trade-off** Wide bins hide tail detail. Disclose edges; use **common edges** for comparisons. Adaptive means data-dependent, not changing per observation.

R lab: change bin width, not the observations

Same 100 synthetic two-cluster responses; only binning changes.

  • Run: read both axes; inspect bin counts.
  • Change: set bin_width from 4 to 40. Run again.
  • Explain: which structure disappears without changing observations?

==Check: all bin counts still sum to 100.==

May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

  if (requireNamespace("webr", quietly = TRUE)) webr::install("ggplot2")
  else stop("Install ggplot2 first")
}
library(ggplot2)
x <- c(
  36.203861904595, 36.968344965996, 37.373171342811, 37.663249348955, 37.894944427129, 38.090935235275, 38.262750520860, 38.417100222768, 38.558256085355, 38.689118543731,
