<-, $, [, [[, +, if / else, ! and ::
**<-** assigns; **$** selects a column; **[** subsets; **[[** extracts a list element. **+** adds plot layers; **if/else** branches; **!** negates; **::** selects a package function.

A bin-free view of the frequency distribution?

**Same data, different histograms** Bin width and origin change the picture, not the data. We want an empirical distribution view **without those choices**. - **Parameter-free counting:** no bins, bandwidth or assumed distribution family. - **Cumulative:** at each value, report the fraction **at or below it**. - **Objective for the same data:** no subjective bin selection; sampling bias and measurement limits remain. ==The ECDF accumulates frequencies. It is not a density curve.==

ECDF: one cumulative count for every threshold

**Empirical cumulative distribution function** For each x, count every observation with xᵢ ≤ x and divide by n. The indicator in the formula is **1 when the condition holds, otherwise 0**. - Sort the data, retaining identities and ties. - At each observed value, add its multiplicity/n. - Hold the fraction constant until the next value. ==No bins, no fitted population model.== Below the minimum the ECDF is 0; at and above the maximum it is 1. It includes the jump at x: **right-continuity**.
F_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{x_i\le x\}
Fₙ(x) and x
Fₙ(x): unitless sample fraction at or below threshold x. The threshold x has the measurement unit.
xᵢ, n, i and Σ
xᵢ: observed value i; n: sample size; i: index 1 to n; Σ: sum over every observation, including ties.
1{xᵢ ≤ x}
Indicator: 1 when xᵢ ≤ x, otherwise 0. Equality is included: tied values enter together. Dividing the count by n gives the fraction.

Calculate an ECDF: include every tie

**Seven-value hand calculation** Sorted synthetic concentrations: **2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7 mg/L**. - At x = 3.9: 1 value included → **1/7**. - At x = 4: both tied 4s enter → **3/7**. - At x = 4.1: no new value → still **3/7**. The jump at 4 is **2/7**, not 1/7. Filled endpoints are included; open endpoints are left limits. The vertical connector is not a set of intermediate function values.

Answer the river question exactly

**Scenario** 50 constructed river concentrations: 0.5, 1.0, …, 25.0 mg/L. Not environmental evidence. **Interpretation** At **12.3 mg/L**, 24 observations are included: **24/50 = 48%**. There are no observations between 12 and 12.5, so this segment is flat. At 12.5: **25/50 = 50%**. For an interval (a,b], subtract Fₙ(a) from Fₙ(b). This is an observed sample fraction, not an estimate with guaranteed precision or a regulatory conclusion.

Different shapes, identical mean and SD

**Scenario: four synthetic detector series** 100 observations each; all have mean **50**, sample SD **10 a.u.** **Interpretation** - **Uniform:** nearly steady rise across its range. - **Normal-like:** faster rise near the centre, slower in the tails. - **Right-skewed:** rapid early rise, then a long upper tail. - **Bimodal:** two rising regions separated by a plateau. Steep regions mean many observations in a short interval; a plateau means none in that interval. An ECDF is not a density curve.

Crossing curves: which series is higher depends on x

**Scenario: compare response distributions** Focus on the uniform and normal-like series, each n = 100. Compare the curves below and above 50 a.u. **Interpretation** Their curves cross: one can include a larger fraction at a low threshold and a smaller fraction at a higher threshold. ==No single mean or universal ranking answers every threshold question.== A higher ECDF at x means **more values ≤ x**, not larger measurement values. This descriptive comparison is not a significance test or proof that one analytical method is better.

Read backwards: inverse ECDF versus linear interpolation

**Scenario: the same 50 river samples** Ask for the smallest observed x with Fₙ(x) ≥ **.25**. It is observation ceil(50 × .25) = **rank 13**, hence **6.5 mg/L**. **Interpretation** The generalized inverse selects an observed value. Linear interpolation instead uses h = 1 + 49 × .25 = **13.25**, between 6.5 and 7: **6.625 mg/L**. ==Both conventions are explicit, but they are not identical.== At p = 0, software conventions need separate care; the generalized inverse here is defined for 0 < p ≤ 1.

First moment: the mean locates the data

**Meaning** The arithmetic mean is the first raw moment: the balancing point of equally weighted observations. It uses the measurement unit. **Compare three shapes** 100 synthetic values each: uniform, normal-like and strongly right-skewed. All have mean **50 a.u.**, despite different shapes. The next 3×3 panel shows the **same series** as points, a boxplot and a histogram. A cyan line marks the mean in every subplot. **Limit:** the mean need not be a typical observation and is sensitive to extremes. It does not reveal spread or shape.
\begin{gathered}\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\\bar{x}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\end{gathered}
X, xᵢ, i and n
X: random measurement variable; xᵢ: observed value i; i: index 1 to n; n: sample size.
μ and x̄
μ: population mean; x̄: mean of this sample. Both use the measurement unit; an observed x̄ need not equal μ.
E[ ], Σ and 1/n
E[ ]: probability-weighted population expectation, requiring a finite first absolute moment. Σ adds observations i = 1 to n; 1/n forms their empirical average.

Mean: one centre, three distributions and three views

Second central moment: variance measures squared spread

**Meaning** Centre each value on the mean, square the deviation, then average. The result has **squared measurement units** and is unchanged by an additive offset. **Keep conventions explicit** Descriptive variance **m₂ uses n**. Sample variance **s² uses n−1**. For our 100-reading series, m₂ = **99 a.u.²** and s² = **100 a.u.²**. The next panels shade **mean ± √m₂**, a scale guide in a.u., not variance itself or a fixed-coverage interval. **Limit:** identical variance can accompany very different shapes; squaring gives extremes substantial influence.
\begin{gathered}\sigma^2=\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^2],\quad\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\m_2=\frac1n\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2=\frac{n-1}{n}s^2\end{gathered}
X, μ, E[ ] and σ²
X: random measurement; μ: its expectation; E[ ]: population expectation; σ²: population variance. A finite second moment is required.
m₂ and s²
m₂: empirical variance with divisor n; s²: sample variance with n−1. Their relation requires n > 1. All variances have squared measurement units.
xᵢ, x̄, n, i and Σ
xᵢ: observed value i; x̄: sample mean; n: sample size; i: index 1 to n; Σ: sum over those observations. The empirical squared deviations concern this sample, not a known population σ².

Variance: identical squared spread does not identify shape

Skewness: balance of signed cubic deviations

**Meaning** Skewness standardizes the third central moment. Positive values mean stronger positive cubic contributions; negative values mean stronger negative contributions. It is **dimensionless**. **Compare three shapes** Uniform and normal-like: g₁ ≈ **0**. Right-skewed: g₁ ≈ **1.759**, with mean 50 above median 46.919 a.u. The next panels mark **mean in cyan**, **median in dashed violet**. Point size shows cubic-contribution magnitude; violet/orange distinguishes negative/positive deviations. The coefficient itself is printed, not placed on the measurement axis. **Limit:** zero skewness does not establish symmetry or a normal distribution.
\begin{gathered}\gamma_1=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^3]}{\sigma^3},\quad\sigma>0\\g_1=\frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}
γ₁ and g₁
γ₁: population skewness; g₁: descriptive sample counterpart. Both are dimensionless; no small-sample bias adjustment is applied to g₁.
E[ ], X, μ and σ
E[ ]: population expectation; X: random measurement; μ: population mean; σ: population SD. A finite third absolute moment and σ > 0 are required.
m₃ and m₂
m₃: average cubed deviation from the sample mean; m₂: average squared deviation, each using n. Dividing by m₂^(3/2) removes the cubed unit. g₁ is undefined if m₂ = 0.

Skewness: distinguish positive and negative contributions

Kurtosis: weight of extreme standardized deviations

**Meaning** Kurtosis averages fourth powers of deviations after removing location and scale. It is **dimensionless**, not a horizontal coordinate or an interval. **Compare three shapes** Uniform **K ≈ 1.800**; normal-like **2.834**; right-skewed **6.662**. Excess kurtosis subtracts the normal-population benchmark 3. In the next point plots, larger points indicate larger fourth-power contributions. The cyan band is **mean ± two divisor-n SDs**, only a visual scale guide. **Limit:** kurtosis is not peak height, a mode count or a tail probability. A few extreme values can dominate; m₂ must be positive.
\begin{gathered}\kappa=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^4]}{\sigma^4},\quad\sigma>0\\K=\frac{m_4}{m_2^2},\quad g_2=K-3,\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}
κ, X, μ, σ and E[ ]
κ: population kurtosis; X: random measurement; μ: population mean; σ: population SD; E[ ]: expectation. A finite fourth moment and σ > 0 are required.
K, m₄ and m₂
K: descriptive sample kurtosis. m₄ and m₂ average fourth and squared deviations from the sample mean, using n. K is dimensionless and requires m₂ > 0.
g₂ and 3
g₂: sample excess K−3, without bias correction. Population excess: κ−3; 3 is normal-population kurtosis, not every normal sample's value.

Kurtosis: follow the extreme-deviation contributions

Zero skewness does not imply symmetry

**Exact 50-residual counterexample** 5 residuals equal −3, 25 equal −1, and 20 equal +2 a.u. Mean = (−15−25+40)/50 = **0**. **Calculate** m₃ = [5(−27)+25(−1)+20(8)]/50 = **0**; m₂ = **3**; therefore g₁ = **0**. **But the sample is asymmetric:** −3 has no matching +3 group; +2 has no matching −2 group. Signed cubes cancel without mirror symmetry. ==Inspect the distribution, not just the coefficient.==

R lab: moments, transformations and distribution checks

Three synthetic shapes, 100 values each. Rows compare shapes; columns show points, boxplot, histogram.

  • Run: switch metric: mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis.
  • Change: vary offset, scale_factor, then extreme, one at a time.
  • Explain: what changes? Why does m2 differ from var(x)?

==Geometric guides do not guarantee coverage.==

Base R only. Local execution; no package download.

# Deterministic synthetic grids; same construction as the lecture
p <- ((1:100) - 0.5) / 100
standardize <- function(z) 50 + 10 * as.numeric(scale(z))
series <- list(Uniform=standardize(p), Normal=standardize(qnorm(p)), Skewed=standardize(qexp(p)))
offset <- 0
scale_factor <- 1
extreme <- FALSE
metric <- 'variance'  # mean, variance, kurtosis, skewness
stopifnot(metric %in% c('mean','variance','kurtosis','skewness'))
series <- lapply(series, function(x) offset + scale_factor*x)
if (extreme) series$Normal[100] <- series$Normal[100] + 50

describe <- function(x) {
  d <- x-mean(x); m2 <- mean(d^2)
  c(mean=mean(x), m2=m2, sample_variance=var(x),
    kurtosis=if(m2>0) mean(d^4)/m2^2 else NA_real_,
    skewness=if(m2>0) mean(d^3)/m2^1.5 else NA_real_)
}
print(t(sapply(series, describe)))
x <- series$Normal; m2 <- mean((x-mean(x))^2)
cat('n =',length(x),'; sample variance =',var(x),'; m2 =',m2,'\n')

# Shared measurement axes and histogram edges
limits <- range(unlist(series)); if(diff(limits)==0) limits <- limits+c(-1,1)
edges <- seq(limits[1], limits[2], length.out=17)
mark <- function(x) {
  mu <- mean(x); root_m2 <- sqrt(mean((x-mu)^2))
  abline(v=mu,col='deepskyblue3',lwd=2)
  if(metric=='variance') abline(v=mu+c(-1,1)*root_m2,col='deepskyblue3',lty=3)
  if(metric=='kurtosis') abline(v=mu+c(-2,2)*root_m2,col='orange3',lty=3)
  if(metric=='skewness') abline(v=median(x),col='purple3',lty=2,lwd=2)
}
interpolated_box <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x,c(.25,.5,.75),type=7)
  width <- q[3]-q[1]
  inside <- x[x>=q[1]-1.5*width & x<=q[3]+1.5*width]
  flagged <- x[x<q[1]-1.5*width | x>q[3]+1.5*width]
  plot(NA,xlim=limits,ylim=c(0,1),yaxt='n',ylab='',
       main='Boxplot: linear interpolation',xlab='Response (a.u.)')
  segments(min(inside),.5,max(inside),.5)
  segments(c(min(inside),max(inside)),.4,c(min(inside),max(inside)),.6)
  rect(q[1],.3,q[3],.7,col='lavender',border='purple3')
  segments(q[2],.3,q[2],.7,lwd=2)
  points(flagged,rep(.5,length(flagged)),pch=16,cex=.5,col='orange3')
  mark(x)
  print(c(Q1=q[1],median=q[2],Q3=q[3],
          lower_whisker=min(inside),upper_whisker=max(inside)))
}
par(mfrow=c(3,3),mar=c(3,3,2.8,0.7),cex=0.7)
for(name in names(series)) {
  x <- series[[name]]; result <- describe(x)
  key <- if(metric=='variance') 'm2' else metric
  label <- paste(name,key,'=',round(result[key],3))
  stripchart(x,method='stack',pch=16,cex=0.45,xlim=limits,
             main=label,xlab='Response (a.u.)'); mark(x)
  interpolated_box(x)
  hist(x,breaks=edges,right=FALSE,include.lowest=TRUE,
       main='Histogram: common edges',xlab='Response (a.u.)'); mark(x)
}
cat('Variance guide: mean +/- sqrt(m2); kurtosis guide: mean +/- 2*sqrt(m2). Neither is a universal coverage interval.\n')
a <- rep(c(-3,-1,2),c(5,25,20))
cat('Counterexample: mean =',mean(a),'; m3 =',mean((a-mean(a))^3),'\n')
stopifnot(length(x)==100,isTRUE(all.equal(var(x),mean((x-mean(x))^2)*100/99)))
standardize(z)
Local helper: rescale a synthetic grid to **sample mean 50 and sample SD 10**. Not a fitted population model.
scale(z)
By default subtract the mean and divide by **sample SD**. Returns a matrix with scaling attributes.
as.numeric(...)
Convert the scaled matrix to a plain numeric vector, dropping its matrix shape and attributes.
qnorm(p)
Return standard-normal quantiles at p. Here p is a **deterministic midpoint grid**, not random sampling.
qexp(p)
Return exponential quantiles (default rate 1), supplying the right-skewed grid before standardization.
c(...)
**Combine** values or named results into a vector; does not sort them.
list(...)
Collect the three named series, retaining each as a separate numeric vector.
lapply(series, function(x) ...)
Transform every series by the same offset/scale setting; return a **list** of transformed vectors.
sapply(series, describe)
Run describe() on each series; simplify equally sized result vectors into a matrix.
t(...)
Transpose the summary matrix so each printed **row is one series**.
describe(x)
Local helper: return mean, two variance conventions, skewness and **Pearson kurtosis K, not excess**. Constant data give undefined shape coefficients.
mean(x)
Calculate an arithmetic mean. Averaging powers of centred deviations gives **empirical moments with divisor n**.
var(x)
Calculate **sample variance with divisor n−1**, not descriptive variance with divisor n.
median(x)
Return the middle ordered value, averaging the two middle values for even n. Used for the dashed comparison line.
sqrt(...)
Take the nonnegative square root: convert descriptive variance into a spread guide in the **original unit**.
length(x)
Count vector elements, including ties. Each teaching series should contain 100 observations.
print(...)
Display computed result vectors or matrices explicitly in the text output.
cat(...)
Write labelled values and line breaks to the text output; does not return a table.
unlist(series)
Flatten the list **only to find shared axis limits**; series stay separate for analysis.
range(...)
Return the smallest and largest values across the series, defining shared measurement limits.
diff(limits)
Subtract consecutive values. For two limits this gives the axis width; zero triggers safe plotting expansion.
seq(..., length.out=17)
Generate 17 shared edges spanning the limits, giving **16 histogram bins** in every row.
quantile(x, ..., type=7)
Compute quartiles by **linear interpolation**, not the alternative hinges of some boxplot implementations. The numeric argument selects this calculation in R.
min(inside), max(inside)
**min()** selects the smallest and **max()** the largest observation inside the fences. Those observations end the whiskers.
rep(...)
Repeat point heights or values. A vector of counts sets each value's multiplicity in the asymmetric counterexample.
par(mfrow=c(3,3), ...)
**mfrow** fills nine panels row by row; **mar** sets margins; **cex** sets text/symbol scaling.
names(series)
Return the series names for iteration and labels.
paste(...)
Combine series name, descriptor name and value into a plot title.
round(..., 3)
Round the **displayed label** to three decimals; calculations retain unrounded values.
stripchart(..., method="stack")
Draw individual observations with stacking. Point height is **not time or a second measurement**.
plot(NA, xlim=..., ylim=...)
Create an empty frame for the custom boxplot, with explicit shared limits and axis labels.
segments(...)
Draw line segments for whiskers, end caps and the median.
rect(...)
Draw the box between the explicitly calculated first and third quartiles.
points(...)
Add orange points for observations outside the fences; they remain in the sample.
abline(v=..., col=..., lty=..., lwd=...)
Add vertical reference lines: **v** position, **col** colour, **lty** dash style, **lwd** width. No probability is estimated.
hist(..., breaks=edges, right=FALSE, include.lowest=TRUE)
Use shared explicit bins. **right=FALSE** makes them left-closed; **include.lowest=TRUE** includes the terminal endpoint for this closure.
mark(x)
Local helper: draw the mean and metric-specific guides. **metric** selects the guide, not a new dataset or confidence interval.
interpolated_box(x)
Local helper: draw linearly interpolated quartiles, observed whiskers and flagged points; print their numerical boundaries.
stopifnot(...)
Stop if a check fails. The metric check limits allowed settings; the final check inspects the **last loop series**, not all three.
isTRUE(all.equal(...))
**all.equal()** compares with numerical tolerance, returning TRUE or a diagnostic; **isTRUE()** produces one logical pass/fail value.
function, for, if / else, <-, $, [, [[, %in% and arithmetic
**function** defines helpers; **for** repeats; **if/else** branches. **<-** assigns; **$**, **[**, **[[** select data; **%in%** tests membership. **:** makes integer sequences; + − * / calculate; **^** raises powers. Comparisons return logical values; **& / |** combine them. **NA_real_** marks undefined numeric coefficients.
